items.quote: all that is of the Virtues and pure Truth and Nature of the Elements, which feare not the Fire of Heaven shall remaine like a pure, cleare, incorruptible and fixed Essence in a serene resplendent Chrystalin Earth
items.note: The author says that what is of the virtues, truth and nature of the Elements and does not fear the Fire of Heaven will remain as a pure, incorruptible, fixed Essence in a crystalline Earth, at rest with the saved.

items.quote: carryed upward like an Eagle, or as Smoak excited by the Fire
items.note: Two likenesses for the way this Essence is carried upward: an Eagle, and smoke raised by fire. The text marks them as likenesses with 'like' and 'as'.

items.quote: when God shall change all things by making them new according to his will, and shall make them all like Christall, then the motions of the Supernaturall Nature shall abide in those things without corruption
items.note: The author states that God will make all things new and like crystal, and that the motions of the Supernaturall Nature will then stay in them without corruption.

items.quote: I wish the Great Ones of our time who are sufficiently enriched with Gold and Silver from the revenues of their subjects, would bestow some part of their wealth upon men piously and consciensciously learned and skilfull in Chymistry
items.note: The author's wish: that the rich great men of his time would spend part of their wealth on pious men skilled in Chymistry, each set a task he is fit for.

items.quote: to find out one out of those Three Families of Nature, that out of the same things in which all Physick is founded, viz. Animalls, Vegetables, and Mineralls
items.note: The text names three Families of Nature and lists them: Animalls, Vegetables, Mineralls; it says all Physick is founded in them. Each man's task is to find out one of the three.

items.quote: separating them by Fire into their Three First (things.)
items.note: The step of work named: the choice Physicall Mysteries fetched out of animals, vegetables and minerals are separated by Fire into their Three First. The word '(things.)' stands in brackets in the text.

items.quote: All beauty, corporeal and incorporeall is nothing else but the splendor of the Divine countenance and Light set in created things
items.note: The margin note says what beauty is: the splendor of the Divine countenance and Light set in created things, shining out through fair bodies.

items.quote: For so much Light as a King hath in him, so much Majesty hath he. Quantum Luminis, tantum Numinis.
items.note: The note measures a King's Majesty by the Light in him and adds a Latin line that it leaves in Latin.

items.quote: The Phylosophicall Conclave of any Prince furnished with such most precious and wholesome a Treasure, might compare even with the riches of Pactolus
items.what: The Phylosophicall Conclave of any Prince
items.note: The text names a prince's Phylosophicall Conclave, furnished with this Treasure, and sets it beside the riches of Pactolus.

items.quote: attract the eyes of the spectators to contemplate the open riches of secret Nature
items.note: Nature is called secret, and the collection is said to lay her riches open to the eyes of those who look.

items.quote: what admirable elevation of the mind would it cause to the Creator himselfe
items.note: The author holds that beholding this beauty would refresh the eyes and lift the mind to the Creator.

items.quote: the Vegetables answering to the members of our body by an Harmonicall Anatomy
items.note: The author says the Vegetables answer to the members of the human body, and calls this an Harmonicall Anatomy.

items.quote: in their Three First (principles) with their garments put off; made naked and visible
items.note: The Three First are spoken of as stripped of garments and made naked and visible: a figure of clothing for what covers them. The word '(principles)' stands in brackets in the text.

items.quote: the TRIUNE naked DIANA shining with so many colours of variety and alwayes with a Triple Form in every classis or distribution
items.note: With 'viz.' the text gives the name TRIUNE naked DIANA to what is seen of vegetables, animals, minerals and metals in their Three First; she has a Triple Form in every class.

items.quote: a most limpid or clear MERCURIAL, a most garnished SULPHUREAN or oyly, and a most bright pure SALINE form
items.note: The Triple Form is spelled out as three forms: MERCURIAL (limpid or clear), SULPHUREAN (or oily), SALINE (bright, pure).

items.quote: who otherwise covereth her selfe from the dishonest looks of mortalls, and desireth not to come into the company of men in this worldly scene with her veile
items.note: The text says this DIANA otherwise covers herself from the dishonest looks of mortals and does not wish to come among men.

items.quote: A work truly becoming a great King and Prince.
items.note: The author judges this work fit for a great King and Prince.

items.quote: Francis the First King of France, the greatest Favorer of Phylosophers and learned men, intended to go about one of the Three, but was prevented by death.
items.note: The author reports that Francis the First of France meant to undertake one of the Three and died before he did. 'One of the Three' takes up the three named in CH6.30.

items.quote: the sole fountaine being reserved to it selfe for its own uses, but by drawing forth spare streams
items.note: A figure of a fountain and its spare streams: the one source is kept for its own uses and only what is spare is drawn off. The lines given do not say plainly what the fountain is.

items.quote: the duty of an Almoner in this great Hospitall of Piety most worthy of all praise and eternall memory, to do good to God, with this Talent, in our poor neighbour and his members?
items.note: The author puts as a question that it is a work of humanity and an almoner's duty to do good with this Talent to the poor neighbour.

items.quote: the Father of Lights (from onely as from the Efficient, Principall, and Finall Cause of all Creatures and Operations, every good Gift upon amendment of Life is by asking, seeking, and knocking, to be obtained)
items.note: The author names God the Father of Lights and the Efficient, Principall and Finall Cause; every good Gift is to be had from him upon amendment of life, by asking, seeking and knocking.

items.quote: would load this pious and laudable purpose heap upon heap with far greater and perhaps unlookt for blessings
items.note: The author holds that God would add greater blessings to those who go this way in the Fear of God and love of their neighbour.

items.quote: By the Light of God, secret and hidden things are revealed and made manifest.
items.note: The margin note says secret and hidden things are made manifest by the Light of God, and that nothing good and perfect is attained without him.

items.name: Psal. 145.19. Prov. 10.24.
items.note: The note names two places of scripture beside the passage on God performing the will of them that fear him.

items.quote: For this onely is the Kings high-way, not onely to come all the desired Secrets of Nature, but that which is the chiefest thing of all it leadeth even to the very workmaster of the universe,
items.note: The text names the way just described (in the Fear of God and love of the neighbour, CH6.34) the only Kings high-way, both to the Secrets of Nature and to the workmaster of the universe.

items.quote: by which ONE infinite OCEAN of all Divine GOODNES through Regeneration (alterity being swallowed up of unity) in the Sabath of Sabbaths or when the eternal Jubile is come for which we were created
items.note: The author says that through Regeneration, otherness being swallowed up by unity, we reach the mark for which we were created, in the Sabath of Sabbaths or eternal Jubile.

items.quote: just like a miserable Exile and pilgrim (tossed up and down through various hazards, hardships, streights, and miserable sufferings) restord againe to his rightful Country
items.note: A likeness, marked by 'just like': the one who attains is as an exile and pilgrim restored to his rightful country.

items.quote: There is no recovering or returning to what we have lost but by the Crosse and Death
items.note: The author states that what was lost is recovered only by the Crosse and Death.

items.quote: but through the Fire of Temptation and Tribulation, with a sad and sharpe death, because the Coronation and wiping away of all teares is after the victory
items.note: The author says God will not have man come to blessedness by a delicate journey, but through the Fire of Temptation and Tribulation. Fire here is the text's word for temptation and tribulation.

items.quote: He that knows One knows All things, he that Earneth many things learneth nothing Eccl. 34.12, 13, 14.
items.name: Eccl. 34.12, 13, 14.
items.note: A saying on knowing One and so knowing All, with a place of scripture named straight after it; the note does not say outright that the saying is taken from that place.

items.quote: Blessednesse consisteth in the apprehension of the chiefest good.
items.note: The note says what Blessednesse consists in: apprehending the chiefest good.

items.quote: God is the Immutable Rest, after which every Creature doth gaspe and groan with all its endeavor.
items.note: The note calls God the Immutable Rest that every creature strives after.

items.quote: Levit. 25. Tob. 12.13. Eccl. 2.5. Prov 17.3.
items.name: Levit. 25. Tob. 12.13. Eccl. 2.5. Prov 17.3.
items.note: The note names four places of scripture beside the passage on the Jubile and on trial by fire and tribulation.

items.quote: We cannot get the Victory and Crown of Patience without striving & fighting.
items.note: The note says victory and the crown of patience come only by striving and fighting. A Latin line follows it in the note, left in Latin, with two letters the transcription could not read.

items.quote: But, to returne to the supream
items.note: The author says he returns to 'the supream', a matter taken up earlier in this writing; the lines given do not show the earlier place.

items.quote: many times though in vaine aspiring and earnestly desiring to enter into the inner rooms of that supream Phylosophicall Oratory
items.note: The supreme matter is spoken of as an Oratory with inner rooms; the author says he has often desired to enter them, in vain.

items.quote: not to the end that I might make Gold and Silver, for truely they are rich enough who are content with a little and make it not their businesse to get much
items.note: The author says his aim was not to make Gold and Silver.

items.quote: but with an exceeding love to find out the True Physick and upright desire of the wonderfull works of God
items.note: The author gives his aim as his own: love of finding the True Physick and desire of the works of God.

items.quote: by so much the more bitterly have I been worryed hitherto by the slanderous Envy of malevolent men, and waves or fruits of of Fortune
items.note: The author says the more he followed these most secret Studies, the more he was troubled by the envy of ill-willing men and by Fortune.

items.quote: though I cannot proceed further as yet, I comfort my selfe with the cogitation onely, and thinking upon so great a Thing
items.note: The author says of himself that he cannot go further as yet and has only the thought of so great a Thing.

items.quote: God himselfe knoweth what, to whom, when and how is fit
items.note: The author leaves to God what is given, to whom, when and how.

items.quote: on whom God bestoweth somethings as a punishment when he is angry, which he denies as a blessing when he is pleased
items.note: The author holds that God gives some things as punishment and withholds them as a blessing, and that the life of those whose felicity is their ruin is not to be desired.

items.name: Num. 11.33. Psal. 78.30, 31, & 104. & 105. Tob. 12.7.
items.note: The note names places of scripture beside the passage on what God turns away or bestows.

items.quote: the works of God are to be published and celebrated
items.note: The author states that the works of God are to be made public and praised, and gives this as his reason for telling what follows.

items.quote: by this monument here left it may hereafter appear that that Divine Benificence hath not been denyed to men of our age also
items.note: The author calls what he here leaves a monument, to show later times that the Divine Benificence was not denied to men of his own age.

items.quote: was shewed to me as an eye-witnesse in my travells, which was denyed to many others who earnestly desired it, that I should see and taste it, at some Great mans house
items.note: The author says that in his travels, at a great man's house, he saw and tasted it as an eye-witness, a thing denied to many others. The house is not named in English.

items.quote: Cui in aeternum bene sIt, & Cumprimis egregium Helioch Antharum bor EaLem, nunc in Christo quiescentem: cujuSmodi lENtis DenIque consueVerunt latitare tempOrum currIcVlis. Which I forbear to English.
items.note: Where the great man would be named the text goes into Latin, and the words 'Which I forbear to English' say it is left untranslated on purpose. The lines given do not show whose 'I' this is.

items.quote: cujuSmodi lENtis DenIque consueVerunt latitare tempOrum currIcVlis
items.note: In the Latin lines capital letters stand inside words (also 'sIt' and 'EaLem' before this), unlike the printing around them. The text does not say what they are for.

items.quote: Whence being a long time astonished and amazed at the greatest miracle of Nature wrought by Art
items.what: the greatest miracle of Nature wrought by Art
items.note: The text names what the author witnessed the greatest miracle of Nature wrought by Art.

items.quote: the various and manifold metamorphosis of the Inferior Astronomy made in the cold
items.note: The text names the Inferior Astronomy and says its many changes were made in the cold.

items.quote: the Moyst way of the Ancients not as yet intensly exalted to the eye of the Basilisk
items.what: the Moyst way of the Ancients
items.note: The text names the Moyst way of the Ancients and says that in what he saw it was not yet raised to 'the eye of the Basilisk', a further degree named but not explained in this paragraph.

items.quote: by giving one onely drop of that Latex or liquor
items.note: The step described: one single drop of the Latex or liquor is given to a sick man.

items.quote: in which as in a storehouse the dispersed vertues of all Celestiall and Terrestriall bodies were by a wonderfull artifice invisibly gathered together in an heap, nay, in which the whole world was centred
items.note: The text says what this liquor is: a storehouse in which the scattered virtues of all heavenly and earthly bodies are gathered invisibly by art, in which the whole world is centred.

items.quote: a man desperately sick and at the point of death was recovered by its Fiery, Astrall, and Celestiall Invisible Nature conveying to the Heart a beam of the Naturall Life
items.note: The author reports the result he saw: a dying man recovered, the liquor's fiery, astral, invisible nature bringing a beam of the Naturall Life to the heart; restored to health in one night.

items.quote: For this Kingly medicine, and the Empresse of all other, causeth Humane Bodies immediately and as it were miraculously to rise againe from what desperate diseases soever,
items.what: this Kingly medicine, and the Empresse of all other
items.note: The text gives the medicine two titles, Kingly medicine and Empresse of all other, and says it raises human bodies from any desperate disease.

items.quote: if God hath not otherwise decreed, for many diseases are a Divine innate punishment, for which there is no cure in Nature.
items.note: The author sets a limit to the medicine: it does not cure where God has decreed otherwise; many diseases are a divine punishment with no cure in Nature.

items.quote: this whole new regenerate world is able by vertue of its Regeneration to renew the little old corruptible world Man
items.note: The medicine is here called a 'whole new regenerate world' and Man a 'little old corruptible world': the word world is used of both, not in its plain sense.

items.quote: reduce the whole Microcosm into a true Temperament, and preserve it therein till the appointed Terme of death imposed on mortalls for their sin
items.note: The author says it brings the whole Microcosm to a true Temperament and keeps it so only until the appointed term of death.

items.quote: The Physophycall Basilisk like Lightning suddenly and unawares burneth up any imperfect mettall whatsoever, and on a sudden Produceth another new forme.
items.note: The margin note says what the Basilisk named in the paragraph does: like lightning it burns up any imperfect metal and at once produces another new form.

items.quote: Therefore the searching it out is most to be commended to all that are studious of the Truth.
items.note: The note commends searching it out to all who study the Truth.

items.quote: There is no Physitian can cure death, but Christ.
items.note: The note says no physician but Christ can cure death.

items.quote: Imperfect and impure mettalls are cleansed from their infirmities and accidents by the same spirit of the world, by the same Heat of Sun and Moon as mens bodies are
items.note: The author says imperfect metals are cleansed by the same spirit of the world and the same Heat of Sun and Moon by which men's bodies are.

items.quote: they are restored to their True Health, which is aureity or goldness
items.note: The text says what the True Health of metals is: aureity or goldness.

items.quote: without a new motion of generation and corruption, by way of alteration onely, and remotion of accidents which are the cause of the sicknesse and distemper
items.note: The author says this restoring is by alteration only and the removal of accidents, with no new generation and corruption.

items.quote: for mettals doe not differ in specie but onely in accidents
items.note: The author's stated ground: metals differ only in accidents, not in kind.

items.quote: No marvell if this secret, by reason of the proclaimed uncertainty of so great mysteries, shall seem incredible, and justly not to be made known (though it be truer then true) to our Vulgar sort
items.note: The author calls it a secret that will seem incredible to the Vulgar sort and is justly not to be made known to them, though he holds it truer than true.

items.quote: as being ignorant because they never heard any thing in all their life of the Heat of the Sun and Moon
items.note: The author says the Vulgar sort are ignorant because they have never heard of the Heat of the Sun and Moon.
items.term: Heat of the Sun and Moon

items.quote: who know not these Vulcanean metamorphoses and this Power of GOD joyned to Nature, but admire the Heathenish Physick
items.note: The text names the changes spoken of Vulcanean metamorphoses and a Power of GOD joined to Nature, and sets against them the Heathenish Physick that the Vulgar admire.

items.quote: account the sayings of Prudent men but as fables and fictions
items.name: our Vulgar sort
items.note: A judgement the author reports of the Vulgar sort in order to reject it: that the sayings of prudent men are fables and fictions.

items.quote: the understanding of the intelligent, clouded with no precepts or traditions of foolish men, can hardly apprehend it
items.note: The author says even the intelligent can hardly grasp it.

items.quote: much lesse that the Element of EARTH should by the help of Mechanick Magick swim upon the water
items.note: A further thing said to be still harder to grasp: that the Element of EARTH swims upon the water by Mechanick Magick. The lines given do not explain it.

items.quote: This incredulous doubtfulnesse will fall out to the gaine rather than to the losse
items.note: The margin note counts the general disbelief a gain: few believe the Art is true.

items.quote: for upon that account God provideth for the security of those that give themselves truly to the study of Phylosophy
items.note: The note says that by this disbelief God provides for the safety of those who truly study Phylosophy.

items.name: Exod. 32.20. Job 14.19.
items.note: The note names two places of scripture at its end.

items.quote: To know this Phylosophicall Secret truly is principally necessary to an Astrall Physitian
items.note: The author holds that an Astrall Physitian must know this Phylosophicall Secret, or he cannot be certain in his Art.

items.quote: the four Monarchs of all diseases, the Epilepsie, Gout, Dropsie, Leprosie
items.what: the four Monarchs of all diseases
items.note: The text names four diseases as the four Monarchs of all diseases and lists them.

items.quote: through the help of Christ, not of the Devill, cured by a wonderfull Art, proving in some of his works that God taught him the medicine
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The author says Paracelsus cured these four diseases by the help of Christ, and that Paracelsus proves in some of his works that God taught him the medicine. The works are not named here.

items.quote: he did it not by our common ordinary medicines, but by Restoring or regenerating ones, which are known to very few
items.note: The medicines used are called Restoring or regenerating ones and said to be known to very few.

items.quote: by which Nature being renewed afterward of her own accord she expelleth all things that offend her
items.note: How these medicines are said to work: Nature is renewed and then of herself drives out what offends her.

items.quote: as his Epitaph at Salisburg doth truly and sufficiently witnesse to posterity
items.name: his Epitaph at Salisburg
items.note: The author calls Paracelsus's Epitaph at Salisburg as witness; its words are not given.

items.quote: It is not Christian-like to ascribe to the Devill a greater possibility and power, than to the Infinite divine Wisdome & omnipotence.
items.note: The note argues against ascribing such cures to the Devil.

items.quote: The chiefe Foundation & Scope of true Physitians, because it is not the first but second birth that produceth it.
items.note: The note calls it the chief foundation and aim of true Physitians, and says it is produced by the second birth, not the first.

items.quote: All diseases proceeding from the corruption of humors, how great and desperate soever their cures be, are healed by this universall medicine
items.note: The text names it this universall medicine and says it heals all diseases that come from the corruption of humors.

items.quote: as a Carpenter that squareth all kind of timber
items.note: A likeness, marked by 'as': the one medicine for all diseases is like a carpenter who squares every kind of timber.

items.quote: except the party be at the utmost Terme appointed him by the supream Being; or the disease be inflicted by God, besides Nature, as a punishment and speciall affliction
items.note: Two exceptions the author states: the appointed end of life, and a disease sent by God as punishment.

items.quote: as hath been said
items.note: The author points back to an earlier place in this writing where the same was said; the lines given do not show which.

items.quote: can make use of this peculiar and celestiall Gift, but he on whom God himselfe hath bestowed it
items.note: The author says only one to whom God has given this Gift can make use of it.

items.quote: who onely both inlightneth the obscurity, and darkneth the clearnesse of these mysteries, so that none can understand the plainest things, except he enlighten them, nor be ignorant of the darkest if he illustrate them
items.note: The text says God alone both lights up what is obscure in these mysteries and darkens what is clear: without him the plainest is not understood, with him the darkest is.

items.quote: Lullius that Divine and most perfect Phylosopher, rightly concluded, that between the Artist and God the first cause, there ought to be an agreement without contrariety
items.name: Lullius
items.note: A conclusion the text gives to Lullius and approves: Artist and God, the first cause, must agree without contrariety.

items.quote: that he may open to him what is hid in the magistery of this Art
items.note: Still within what is given to Lullius: the first mover moves the Artist's soul to understanding so as to open to him what is hidden in the magistery of this Art.

items.quote: Blessed will he be to whom the Lord God shall be pleased to inspire the Gifts of his Grace
items.note: The author calls blessed the one whom God inspires with the Gifts of his Grace.

items.quote: but also against their undeserving neighbour by strange devices not becoming an Aedpt Phylosopher
items.note: The author says men sometimes offend against God by ingratitude and against their neighbour by devices not fitting an Adept Phylosopher (the text prints 'Aedpt').

items.quote: some eminent men heretofore and two publick Phylosophers of divers Nations in our time abusing the Gifts of God against those most horrid Anathema's of Phylosophers
items.note: The author speaks of some eminent men of the past and two publick Phylosophers of his own time, unnamed, who abused the Gifts of God against the Anathema's of Phylosophers.

items.quote: every man according to his dexterity which the sydereall spirit causeth and exciteth is the forger of his own fortune
items.note: A view put in brackets with 'doubtlesse': each man forges his own fortune according to the dexterity the sydereall spirit stirs in him.

items.quote: they came to dolefull and lamentable end, to the perpetuall reproach of their Name answerable to the unworthy publishing of this most True Phylosophicall Art
items.note: The text says these men came to a lamentable end that answered to their unworthy making public of the Art.

items.quote: the unworthy publishing of this most True Phylosophicall Art
items.note: Here publishing the Art is called unworthy and is punished; CH6.37 says the works of God are to be published and celebrated. The text calls the publishing here 'unworthy', which may be the difference it means.

items.quote: as also for their cheating Impostures of the first Hapocraticall silence,
items.note: They are said to be punished both for 'provoking loquacity' and for cheating Impostures of the Hapocraticall silence, which the text says they did by turns to cloak the matter for their safety.

items.quote: The originall of the Philosophicall Magistery.
items.what: The originall of the Philosophicall Magistery
items.note: The margin note heads the passage as the origin of the Philosophicall Magistery.

items.quote: Most doe otherwise now, who make thir boast among others that they have the clear knowledge of it, when it is only but imaginary
items.note: The note says most now boast of a clear knowledge that is only imagined, and so hinder themselves from learning more.

items.quote: Those more ancient and skilfull Phylosophers who were born in a happy signe, the children of Hermes who first found out the science
items.note: The text names the more ancient Phylosophers the children of Hermes and says they first found out the science.

items.quote: have even judged it a thing more safely worth their labor to have it indeed without the witnesse of a sottish ignorant multitude, then seeme or be supposed onely to have it
items.note: The ancient Phylosophers are said to have judged it safer to have it in fact, without the multitude as witness, than to seem to have it.

items.quote: not as many too credulous imagine, that being deceived with their own vaine imaginations they would deceive others in like manner
items.name: many too credulous
items.note: A view the author reports in order to reject it: that the ancient Phylosophers, themselves deceived, meant to deceive others.

items.quote: these private not publick Secretaries of Nature
items.what: private not publick Secretaries of Nature
items.note: The text names the ancient Phylosophers private, not publick, Secretaries of Nature.

items.quote: who have, in the Naturall Light fresh and flourishing in them, followed Reason the best guide, according to the ability God gave them
items.note: The author says they followed Reason as the best guide, in the Naturall Light that was fresh in them.

items.quote: accounting nothing more glorious than that they might peaceably rejoyce prudently and in Quiet Silence, with a Mind truly Sound in a Sound Body
items.note: Their aim is given as rejoicing peaceably and in Quiet Silence, sound in mind and body, in the Fear of God and Love of their Neighbour.

items.quote: In the first age of the world God made it known by the Light of Nature.
items.note: The note says God made it known in the first age of the world by the Light of Nature.

items.quote: This is Phylosophy Adept, which Paracelsus in the Tincture of Physicks explaineth them to be Long Life and free from all infirmity, even till the Naturall death
items.note: The text says what Phylosophy Adept is, on the word of Paracelsus in a writing it names the Tincture of Physicks: long life free from infirmity until natural death.

items.quote: an honest support of that long life in this vale of miseries, that we might serve God without poverty and prejudice of our Neighbour
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The second part of what is given to Paracelsus in the Tincture of Physicks: an honest support of that long life, to serve God without poverty.

items.quote: by a wonderfull and most abstruse comprehending of all the vertues of the whole Creation flowing and running together in one certaine masse
items.note: The text says those who seek this happiness have been persuaded it is reached by no other means or arts than a most hidden gathering of all the virtues of the whole Creation into one mass.

items.quote: in this Rode or Kings Highway and Phylosophical Reason is to be accomplished
items.note: The name Kings Highway stands here again, joined with Phylosophical Reason; at CH6.35 'the Kings high-way' is the name given to the way of the Fear of God and love of the neighbour.

items.quote: All these spirituall virtues and active qualities being by great help of ingenuity and Art like the lesser world heaped up together and concentred into one masse
items.note: What is done: all the spiritual virtues and active qualities are heaped together and brought to a centre in one mass by ingenuity and Art, 'like the lesser world'.

items.quote: for the Light of Nature is glittering in the Darknesse of the world
items.note: The author's bracketed remark beside the 'illustration of the Mind' that they have: the Light of Nature shines in the darkness of the world.

items.quote: as also the knowledge of all Naturall things and Heavenly seerets, and a perfect operation
items.note: What those who have it are said to gain besides the lighting of the mind: knowledge of all natural things and heavenly secrets, and a perfect operation.

items.quote: they have even miraculously use of this choycest and admirable Magisterie, together with a flowing plenty and Abundance of all Things
items.note: The text names it this choicest Magisterie; those who have its use have with it abundance of all things.

items.quote: The defect of Nature must be supplyed by the industry of Art
items.note: The margin note says Art must supply what Nature lacks, since Nature always strives toward perfection.

items.quote: Prov. 3.16.
items.name: Prov. 3.16.
items.note: The note names a place of scripture beside the passage on the mind's lighting and abundance of all things.

items.quote: the Phylosophers our predecessors that have been train'd up in Hermes school,
items.note: The text names the earlier Phylosophers as trained in Hermes school.

items.quote: though they have been altogether dumb in keeping close the secret of the Art by a constant Taciturnity
items.note: The text says these Phylosophers kept the secret of the Art by constant silence.

items.quote: knowing to what dangers the searchers out of difficult Arts and the publick Secretaries of Nature are obnoxious, that, full of despaire concerning their safety and peace, they have been compelled to deny the same
items.note: The reason given for their silence: the dangers that searchers of difficult Arts and publick Secretaries of Nature are exposed to, such that they have been forced to deny it.

items.quote: yet usually give this Reason: because the greatest Medicine, being artificially prepared with the help of wise Nature the Mistresse of Science, should be (or is) the Life and inlightning Light
items.name: the Phylosophers our predecessors that have been train'd up in Hermes school
items.note: The reason that follows is given as the one these Phylosophers usually give: the greatest Medicine, prepared by art with Nature's help, is the Life and the enlightening Light.

items.quote: our Balsom, that is, the spirit or celestiall
items.note: With 'that is' the text says what 'our Balsom' means: the spirit, or celestial, not visible vapour of life (the quote stops at a printer's mark in the line); the Medicine is what quickens it.

items.quote: it may be the Essence of our Life
items.note: A hedged statement ('it may be'): the Medicine may be the Essence of our Life.

items.quote: the Fift Essence compounded of the four Elements, in which are all the Elements actually, and all their arts, with greatest agreement made equall with true equation according to all possibility of Nature
items.note: The text says what the Fift Essence is: compounded of the four Elements, all of them actually in it, made equal in the greatest agreement.

items.quote: bound together with a golden chaine without any contrariety
items.note: A figure: the Elements in it are bound together with a golden chain.

items.quote: in the curing of diseases and the metamorphosis of Mettalls, like as in Lightning and the eye of a Basilisk, as is manifest by Experience
items.note: The subtle Matter and Form are said to act in curing diseases and changing metals as Lightning and the eye of a Basilisk do; Basilisk is used as a likeness ('like as'), and experience is called as proof.

items.quote: This is so in respect of the four qualities of the body as the Heaven is incorruptible in respect of the four Elements.
items.note: A proportion the text states: this stands to the four qualities of the body as the incorruptible Heaven stands to the four Elements.

items.quote: They durst not under paine of Anathema to speak of it, but in a picture of Aenigmaticall words, because the Master of Nature gave them not leave
items.note: The margin note says they dared speak of it only in a picture of riddling words, under pain of Anathema, because the Master of Nature gave no leave.

items.quote: lest they should indanger themselves, and give an occasion to others of a wicked & hurtfull study or practice
items.note: Two reasons the note gives for the covered speech: their own danger, and giving others occasion for a wicked and hurtful practice.

items.name: Prov. 10.10.
items.note: The note names a place of scripture after its words on covered speech.

items.quote: It exciteth motion in our bodies and reviveth the Elements
items.note: The note says what the Medicine does in the body: it stirs motion and revives the Elements.

items.quote: the Naturall life is nothing else but the actings of the Elements
items.note: The note says what the Naturall life is: the actings of the Elements.
